title: Renaissance
summary: Renaissance means 're-birth': the revival of art, architecture and literature from the 14th to the 17th century. It began with renewed interest in the classical culture of the Greeks and Romans and was a period of new experiments, power of reasoning, laws and discoveries – the 'Age of Enlightenment'. It spread from Early Renaissance to High Renaissance and finally to Mannerism and Baroque. The 14th-century artists Duccio and Masaccio still used a Gothic method of narration with less anatomy knowledge but showed a sense of scientific proportion and observation. The 15th century stressed balance and harmony of art and nature; the use of light, shadow, foreshortening and perspective was perfected; the most famous painters were Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael and Michelangelo. Mannerist artists extended the principles of the High Renaissance and made elongated figures in illogical spaces, stressing the human soul with an anatomically correct body. Common features: anatomically correct human body, perspective, foreshortening, pyramidal composition and dramatic play of light. Famous artists: Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo, Rembrandt and Rubens.

Artist: Sandro Botticelli. Medium: tempera on canvas. Period: 1485–86. Style: Renaissance. Collection: Galleria degli Uffizi, Florence. It shows a rebirth of classical motifs inspired by 2nd-century Greek masterpieces. The goddess Venus emerges from the water on a shell; the nude goddess represents spiritual, not earthly, love, arriving as a full-grown woman symbolising beauty and truth. A goddess of the seasons offers her cloth embroidered with flowers; on the other side wind gods like angels float in the air. Venus stands in the centre in a modest pose that recalls ancient sculptures; her anatomy is not strictly classical – she has an elongated neck, a left shoulder that slopes at an unusual angle and slim long limbs; the cool, artificial light adds soft, harmonious beauty.

Artist: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), an Italian painter regarded both as scientist and artist (other famous works: The Last Supper, The Virgin of the Rocks). Medium: oil on poplar wood. Period: 16th century. Style: Renaissance. Collection: Louvre Museum, Paris. A woman sits with a mysterious smile that seems to welcome the observer. Leonardo used a pyramid design, in which her folded hands form the base; there is a dramatic contrast of light and dark; the brightly lit face is framed by hair, veil and shadows; eyebrows and eyelashes are missing yet the smile is more striking when looking at the eyes than the mouth. Behind her is a vast landscape of icy mountain, valley and curved river, showing Leonardo's vision of connecting humanity with nature.

Artist: Michelangelo. Medium: marble sculpture from a single slab. Period: 1498–99. Style: Renaissance. Collection: St Peter's, Rome. It shows the Virgin Mary holding the dead body of Christ on her lap (two figures). The structure is pyramidal. Madonna is shown much younger than her son to express her purity. It balances Renaissance ideals of classical beauty with the artist's own creative expression and is his most highly finished work, with unique drapery movements and strong anatomical detail. His other famous works: the sculptures David and Moses and the frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

Artist: Rembrandt, a Dutch realist. Medium: oil on canvas. Period: 1640–42. Style: Renaissance (Baroque). Collection: Rijks Museum, Amsterdam. Rembrandt shows the mysteries in the play of light and shade, which highlights the 'soul' of the painting. A dark varnish gave the wrong impression of a night scene; when it was removed in 1940 the scene was found to be in broad daylight. The young captain, dressed in black with a red sash, gives an order to his lieutenant to march the company of civilians; the lieutenant and a small girl wear yellow, the colour of victory; a white dead chicken at the girl's belt represents the defeated enemy; a drummer in the background energises the march.

vsa: Do you consider 'Monalisa' as the greatest work of art of the Renaissance period?

Yes, because it shows the Renaissance ideals: a pyramid design with the folded hands as the base, dramatic contrast of light and dark, a mysterious smile that welcomes the observer, and a vast landscape behind the figure showing the connection of humanity with nature; it is Leonardo's world-famous masterpiece.
Describe the famous painting 'Birth of Venus'.

Botticelli's Birth of Venus (tempera on canvas, 1485–86, Uffizi, Florence) shows the goddess Venus emerging from the water on a shell, a full-grown nude symbolising spiritual love, beauty and truth; a goddess of the seasons offers her a flowered cloak and wind gods blow from the other side. Her neck is elongated and the light cool and artificial.
Write a note on Sandro Botticelli.

Botticelli was an Italian Renaissance painter whose Birth of Venus (about 1486) is one of the best examples of the rebirth of classical motifs inspired by 2nd-century Greek masterpieces. His figures have elongated necks and limbs and a soft, harmonious beauty with cool light.

Pieta by Michelangelo (marble, 1498–99, St Peter's, Rome) shows the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ on her lap. The structure is pyramidal; Mary is shown young to express purity; the drapery movement and anatomical details are very fine.

sa: What do you mean by the word 'Renaissance'? Explain the main features of this period.

Renaissance means 're-birth', the revival of art, architecture and literature from the 14th to 17th century based on classical Greek and Roman culture. It was an 'Age of Enlightenment' with new experiments, reasoning and discoveries. Features: anatomically correct human body, perfected perspective, foreshortening, light and shadow, balance and harmony, pyramidal composition and dramatic light. It spread from Early and High Renaissance to Mannerism and Baroque.

or: Write an appreciative note on Sandro Botticelli.

Botticelli's Birth of Venus (about 1486, tempera on canvas) shows Venus rising from the sea on a shell as a symbol of spiritual love, beauty and truth, attended by a season goddess and wind gods. Elongated neck and limbs, modest pose recalling ancient sculpture, and soft cool light give it a harmonious, graceful beauty.

sa: Mention the characteristic features of Rembrandt's painting and describe 'The Night Watch'.

Rembrandt was a Dutch realist who used mysterious play of light and shade to highlight the soul of the painting. The Night Watch (1640–42, Rijks Museum) shows a young captain in black with a red sash ordering his lieutenant to march the company; the lieutenant and a small girl wear yellow, the colour of victory; a dead white chicken stands for the defeated enemy and a drummer energises the march. It was thought a night scene because of dark varnish, which was removed in 1940.

Leonardo's Mona Lisa (oil on poplar wood, 16th century, Louvre) shows a woman with a mysterious smile that welcomes the observer. A pyramid design with the folded hands as the base, dramatic contrast of light and dark, a bright face framed by hair, veil and shadow, and a vast background of icy mountain, valley and curved river show the artist's vision of linking humanity with nature.
How did the Renaissance affect painters like Botticelli and Leonardo da Vinci?

The revival of classical ideals made them use anatomy, perspective and light: Botticelli painted classical goddess motifs inspired by Greek masterpieces, and Leonardo used scientific observation, pyramid composition and dramatic light and dark in works like Mona Lisa, The Last Supper and The Virgin of the Rocks.
la: Describe the sculpture 'Pieta' of Michelangelo with its structure and importance.

Pieta (1498–99) is Michelangelo's marble sculpture made from a single slab and kept at St Peter's, Rome. It shows the Virgin Mary seated, holding the dead body of Christ on her lap, in a pyramidal structure with two figures. Madonna is shown much younger than her son to express her purity. It balances Renaissance classical beauty with the artist's expression, has unique drapery movement and strong anatomy and is his most highly finished work.
Explain the painting 'Birth of Venus' by Sandro Botticelli.

Painted about 1486 in tempera on canvas (Uffizi, Florence), it shows the classical goddess Venus emerging from the water on a shell, a nude full-grown woman symbolising spiritual love, beauty and truth. A season goddess offers a flower-embroidered cloth, and wind gods float on the other side. Venus stands in the centre in a modest pose; the anatomy is elongated with a long neck and sloping shoulder; cool artificial light gives soft harmony.

Mona Lisa (oil on poplar wood, 16th century, Louvre) shows a seated woman with a mysterious smile that welcomes the observer, the smile more striking when we look at the eyes. The pyramid design with folded hands as base, the contrast of light and dark, the face framed by hair and veil, and the landscape of mountains, valley and river behind show Leonardo's vision of humanity and nature united.
